newsitem.title: USA: CFTC's Corcoran says bills could raise regulation.
newsitem.headline: CFTC's Corcoran says bills could raise regulation.

text.p: Legislative proposals to revamp the Commodity Exchange Act might actually increase, rather than diminish, regulatory oversight for U.S. markets, Andrea Corcoran, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's director of trading and markets, said Friday.
"These kinds of constraints, however well intentioned, might have an exact opposite effect," Corcoran told a panel discussion at an annual commodities and financial services law institute here.
Members of both the House and Senate have proposed revisions to the act, which governs most U.S. futures trading.
But Corcoran was largely referring to a bill proposed by Representative Thomas Ewing, an Illinois Republican, in late September.
Ewing proposed altering the Treasury amendment to the act to make off-exchange foreign currency dealings only with the general public subject to CFTC regulatory oversight.

"I don't know why that would be a good thing for commercial, sophisticated business, because in the long run if there are a series of problems in that sector, you may end up with a lot more regulation than you counted on," Corcoran said.
"If everyone agrees that fraud is bad and someone should watch the retail market, then...all we are talking about is who is going to do it, not whether it should be done," she added.

The Treasury amendment, which exempts interbank foreign exchange trading from futures regulation, has been interpreted differently and has raised ambiguities. The U.S. Supreme Court will hear a case on this issue on November 13.
Ewing's bill would also exempt from futures regulation trading done by sophisticated traders.

"I guess that means we are precluded from considering the public interest in connection with determining whether or not to apply our exemptive authority, which seems to me very strange," Corcoran said.

She said Ewing's proposal to ensure that the benefits of any new regulations outweigh the costs -- a stricter, more quantitative version of the Senate's bill -- would be a "very high standard to maintain."
"I think that the CFTC has really struggled to take a fair-minded approach...in order to allow the exchanges and OTC (over-the-counter) market to grow," she said.

Corcoran said the commission tries to be as prompt as possible in approving U.S. exchanges' new contracts or products. Both the House and Senate bills proposed shortening the time for CFTC approval on new contracts.

"The reason they take a long time is because they are ill considered and the exchange itself is not ready to trade the contract," she said. -Derivatives desk, 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com
